title: What Is a Theory? Paradigms and Classifications

ctx-obvious.prompt: What is the main lesson of Lazarsfeld’s “obvious” list?
options: All common beliefs about soldiers are wrong.
That a result feels “obvious” once you hear it does not show it was known in advance; common sense can find a reason for any result.
Surveys only confirm what everybody already knows.
The higher the education, the worse the mental health.
ctx-obvious.explain: Lazarsfeld turns the objection “surveys only tell us the obvious” on its head: unless you knew the result beforehand, saying “obvious” is easy. The first option overgeneralises: the author does not say common sense is always wrong, only that it was reversed in these examples. The third option is the very objection he answers, and the fourth states the opposite of the finding (the less educated soldiers showed more symptoms).

ctx-lenses.prompt: A researcher argues that a family watches the evening news to have something to talk about with the neighbours and to keep an eye on what is happening in the world. Which of Meyrowitz’s three narratives is this closest to?
options: Power: the family is crushed under a dominant ideological text.
Pleasure: the family uses the media for ends useful and pleasing to it.
Pattern: what matters is the structure the medium creates.
All three say the same thing, so there is no difference.
ctx-lenses.explain: A view that sees the audience actively using media for its own purposes is close to the “pleasure” narrative. The “power” narrative stresses a dominant ideological text and resistance to it; “pattern” looks at the structure of the medium rather than content. The last option contradicts the starting point of this lesson: the same scene looks different through different glasses.

people-cast.prompt: Which of the following pairings is correct?
people-cast.explain: Kuhn’s The Structure of Scientific Revolutions appeared in 1962 and is tied to the concept of paradigm. Popper is tied to falsifiability, Merton to middle-range theory and Craig to the seven traditions, and their years are 1935, 1949 and 1999 respectively. The pair that gets mixed up most often in exams is Popper–Kuhn: one is about testing theories, the other about how science works socially and historically.

people-contexts.prompt: True or false: the label “administrative research” was Lazarsfeld’s own invention, chosen as praise.
people-contexts.explain: False. According to Pooley and Jeřábek, the label was Adorno’s shorthand for Lazarsfeld’s radio research work, hardly a compliment; Lazarsfeld later adopted it and defended administrative research in his 1941 essay. That is how the label has followed him ever since.

claim-core.prompt: According to McQuail’s broad definition, which of the following can count as a “theory”?
options: Only law-like propositions tested in laboratory experiments
The patterned practical knowledge a news editor has built up from experience
Only explanations produced at universities and published in refereed journals
claim-core.explain: McQuail calls the practical knowledge of media practitioners “operational theory” as long as it is systematic and persistent. The other three options narrow theory: law-like propositions, academic output or numerical relationships are only some kinds of theory, not all.

claim-functions.prompt: A researcher says, “If a topic is heavily shared on social media for a week, its place in the main news bulletins the following week will grow,” and prepares to test it. Which job of theory is being done?
options: The overtime shift of critical theory
claim-functions.explain: The pattern “if this condition, expect that outcome” is prediction and produces a testable inference. Describing would only say “what is,” the normative job says “what ought to be,” and the critical overtime shift aims to expose hidden problems. The sentence here does none of those.

concepts-relatives.prompt: A researcher will test the sentence “the more violence in the evening news, the higher viewers’ fear scores” with survey data collected this week. What does this sentence most resemble?
concepts-relatives.explain: A sentence that states a single relationship in testable form is a hypothesis. A paradigm is the framework and examples shared by a whole community; a model shows a process schematically; a law claims a regularity that holds under all conditions (rare in communication). This sentence does not claim anything that large.

concepts-midrange.prompt: Which of the following fits Merton’s description of middle-range theory?
options: A universal theory deriving every regularity in society from a single system
A set of propositions about a delimited domain (say, reference groups), concrete enough to yield testable hypotheses
The summary table of the data you collected in one study
Only psychological laws that can be established in laboratory experiments
concepts-midrange.explain: Middle-range theory treats a limited domain and can be turned into testable propositions. The first option is what Merton calls a grand unifying effort; the third is not even a theory but plain description; the fourth adds a restriction that is not in Merton’s description.

concepts-mcquail.prompt: A newspaper’s news editor decides which story goes on the front page in the morning meeting, using rules that are never written down but have been applied for years. Which of McQuail’s kinds of theory describes this knowledge?
concepts-mcquail.explain: The knowledge media practitioners accumulate in practice, patterned but often unwritten, is operational theory. Normative theory says “what ought to be,” cultural theory evaluates or questions cultural products, and social scientific theory rests on systematic observation. The editor’s practical knowledge is none of those.

concepts-craig.prompt: A study models how noise distorts a message and how feedback corrects the system. Which of Craig’s traditions is it closest to?
concepts-craig.explain: A study that treats communication as information processing and deals with noise and feedback sits in the cybernetic tradition. The rhetorical tradition centres on the art of discourse, the phenomenological on the experience of the other, and the critical on discursive reflection and questioning power relations.

assumptions-myth.prompt: True or false: according to McQuail, the “dominant paradigm” is a completely neutral approach that contains no value assumptions about society.
assumptions-myth.explain: False. McQuail says a picture of a liberal, pluralist, orderly and well-informed “good society” lies beneath the dominant paradigm, that is, it is essentially normative. A claim of neutrality does not remove the assumption; it only makes it invisible.

assumptions-lenses.prompt: A study interviews 40 viewers in depth to understand what a TV series means to them. Which of Potter, Cooper and Dupagne’s paradigms is it closest to?
options: None; this is not a paradigm
assumptions-lenses.explain: A study that uses qualitative methods to understand how meaning is made is in the interpretive paradigm. The social scientific paradigm centres on quantitative testing, the critical one on power and inequality. The last option is wrong too: these three labels exist precisely to classify studies like this.

assumptions-centric.prompt: A researcher studies how media ownership and control shape the dominant ideology in news. Which of McQuail’s four perspectives is it closest to?
assumptions-centric.explain: The trio of ownership, control and dominant ideology is the signature of the social-materialist view, which treats media as a product of political-economic forces. The media-materialist view focuses on the medium’s technology and organisational dynamics; the culturalist views on subjective meaning and cultural forces. The ownership–ideology link separates them.

how-machine.prompt: Put the steps of Merton’s air-pressure example in the correct order.
items: Image: the atmosphere is a “sea of air”
Inference: pressure on a mountain top should be lower
Test: pressure at the top and the base is compared
Assessment: does the idea generate new questions?
how-machine.explain: The order runs from image to inference, from inference to test, from test to the fruitfulness assessment. Putting measurement before inference is a common mistake: the inference tells you what to measure. Fruitfulness comes last because you can only see whether an idea generates new hypotheses after the tests.

how-popper.prompt: Imagine a theory that says: if the audience is influenced by the news, “there is an effect”; if not, “there is hidden resistance, which is also an effect.” By Popper’s criterion, what can be said of it?
options: It is the strongest theory, because it explains every result.
No observation can refute it, so it is not falsifiable; its scientific testability is weak.
It holds only for news viewers.
how-popper.explain: For Popper, being able to explain every result is the theory’s weakness, not its strength: because it risks nothing, it cannot be tested. The first option catches exactly that fallacy. The third is wrong too: for Popper no theory is conclusively verified, at most it is corroborated by surviving tests.

how-criteria.prompt: A theory explains only the example it started from and generates no other questions or research. Which criterion is it weak on?
how-criteria.explain: Not generating new questions and research is a weakness of heuristic value. Parsimony is about explaining with few assumptions, scope about how many phenomena are covered, falsifiability about being refutable. This theory may be both simple and testable yet still barren.

how-classify.prompt: Match each compass question with the source that frames its answer.
pairs: What kind of theory? (scientific, normative, operational, everyday…)
Where is the action? (media-centric or society-centric)
McQuail: four perspectives on two axes
how-classify.explain: The first and fourth questions both come from McQuail but from different schemes: one gives the kinds of theory, the other the four perspectives on two axes. The pair that gets mixed up most often in exams is Lazarsfeld’s administrative–critical distinction and Craig’s seven traditions: the first looks at whom the research is for, the second at how communication is defined.

evidence-journals.prompt: Which inference from Potter, Cooper and Dupagne’s 1993 count is correct?
options: The social science paradigm was the majority in mainstream journals but could not be called “dominant” in the field as a whole.
Interpretive research was never published in mainstream journals.
All work in the social science line met scientific standards.
evidence-journals.explain: The authors call the social science paradigm the “majority” but not “dominant,” and add that even it did not fully meet the standards. The first option draws a value judgement from a count; the third ignores the roughly 34%; the fourth is the opposite of the authors’ finding.

critique-popper.prompt: Which of the following correctly summarises a criticism of Popper’s falsifiability criterion?
options: When a prediction fails, it can be hard to determine whether the theory or the auxiliary assumptions are wrong.
Popper argued that no theory can ever be supported.
critique-popper.explain: The auxiliary-hypotheses problem shows precisely that one failed prediction does not immediately refute a theory. The first option contradicts the facts; the third turns the criterion upside down; the fourth is wrong too: Popper said theories can be “corroborated” by surviving tests, only that they are never conclusively verified.

critique-maps.prompt: What is the most sensible attitude towards classification schemes (Craig, McQuail and others)?
options: Every theory must be placed in exactly one box.
Schemes are provisional and debatable; use them as a first orientation tool to see what question a theory asks.
Schemes are invalid; theories cannot be classified.
All schemes say the same thing, so one is enough.
critique-maps.explain: Craig calls even his own scheme “tentative”; McQuail says the divisions overlap. So schemes are neither rigid moulds nor worthless. The second option strikes the balance: useful but not exact. The last option is wrong too: each scheme looks along a different axis.

today-tests.prompt: A student says, “Cultivation was the theory of the television age; it is finished.” According to what you have learned in this lesson, which is the best reply?
options: He is right: theories become invalid when technology changes.
That is a testable claim; a 2023 meta-analysis found a relationship in social media studies too, but the shared-message-system assumption must be tested separately in the new environment.
He is wrong: cultivation is automatically valid in every environment.
Theories cannot be tested, so arguing is pointless.
today-tests.explain: The meta-analysis shows the theory being tested in the new environment and a relationship being found, but it is too early to say that this relationship proves the theory’s main assumptions. The first and third options give a verdict too quickly at opposite ends; the fourth rejects the foundation of this lesson: theories are valuable precisely because they can be tested.

today-lab.prompt: A student asks, “Whose algorithm and whose interests does this content serve?” Which of Craig’s traditions is this closest to?
today-lab.explain: Asking in whose interest and inside which power relations is the mark of the critical tradition, which sees communication as discursive reflection and critique. The rhetorical tradition centres on the art of persuasion, the cybernetic on information flow, the phenomenological on lived experience.

turkey-terms.prompt: What does the term “yöndeşme” in Yavuz’s (2015) article mean?
options: The search for a midway and the convergence between the mainstream/pluralist and critical/radical lines
That a theory is specific to one country
The triumph of the social science paradigm
turkey-terms.explain: “Yöndeşme” corresponds to “convergence” in English and describes the search for a midway between two poles. The author says neither tradition is a fixed, unchanging structure and that their common features can be developed; so the triumph, disappearance or country-specificity suggested by the other options is not there.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question asks: “Which concept holds that theories in the social sciences should stand between the small working hypotheses of day-to-day research and grand theories that aim to explain everything?” What is the right answer?
exam-patterns.explain: The position between small hypotheses and grand unifying theories is Merton’s definition of middle-range theory. Popper centres on testability, Kuhn on the examples a scientific community shares, and Craig on seven theoretical traditions of communication.

summary.prompt: True or false: Merton’s concept of middle-range theory says that media effects are of medium size.
summary.explain: False. “Middle-range” concerns the scale and scope of a theory: theories that treat a delimited domain and can be turned into testable propositions. It has nothing to do with whether an effect is small, medium or large.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence best shows the difference between theory and everyday common sense, as in Lazarsfeld’s 1949 “obvious” list?
options: Common sense is always wrong, theory is always right.
Common sense can find a reason for any result after the fact; a theory has to say beforehand which result to expect under which conditions.
Common sense speaks in numbers, theory in words.
There is no difference; theory is dressed-up common sense.
quiz.explain: Lazarsfeld’s game shows how easy it is to say “obvious” when the result was not known beforehand. A theory speaks beforehand, so it can be tested. The first option overreaches with “always”; the third draws the line in the wrong place; the fourth says the opposite of the lesson.

quiz.prompt: True or false: according to Popper, a theory can be conclusively proven by a large number of confirming examples.
quiz.explain: False. For Popper, theories are “corroborated” by surviving tests but never conclusively verified. Falsifiability means the theory is open to observations that could refute it; many compatible examples prove nothing if the theory fits every result.

quiz.prompt: Match the names with their concepts.
quiz.explain: The place these pairings get mixed up is usually Popper and Kuhn: Popper is about the testability of theories, Kuhn about the examples a scientific community shares (the paradigm). Merton frames the scale of theory, Craig the definitions of communication, and Lazarsfeld whom research is done for.

quiz.prompt: Put the works in chronological order (earliest to latest).
items: Lazarsfeld: the administrative and critical research essay (1941)
Merton: Social Theory and Social Structure (1949)
Kuhn: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)
Craig: Communication Theory as a Field (1999)
quiz.explain: The order is 1935, 1941, 1949, 1962, 1999, 2010. Because Popper’s English translation appeared in 1959, that year is often assumed for his first work; the German original is dated 1935. It is also important not to mix up Kuhn’s 1962 with Merton’s 1949.

quiz.text: According to Merton, middle-range theories stand between the small {{1}} produced in abundance in day-to-day research and the {{2}} that aim to explain everything under one roof.
quiz.explain: Middle-range theory lies between small working hypotheses and grand unifying theories. “Paradigm” is Kuhn’s term, not Merton’s; “operational” and “everyday” are McQuail’s kinds of theory. Those options carry the concepts of another lesson.

quiz.scenario: Imagine: a student thinks, “A question mark in a news headline increases the number of clicks.” Over one week the student collects the headlines and click counts of a news site.

parts.prompt: What does this sentence, taken alone, most resemble?
parts.explain: A sentence that states a single relationship in testable form is a hypothesis. A paradigm is a framework shared by a whole scientific community; a normative theory says “what ought to be.”

parts.prompt: Which result would refute this claim?
options: Headlines with question marks not getting higher average clicks than the others
The student not liking the claim
parts.explain: The refuting observation is not seeing the difference the claim predicts. The other options are unrelated to the truth of the claim.

parts.prompt: What is needed to make this claim part of a theory?
options: Connected propositions that explain why this is so and can extend to other situations
parts.explain: A theory contains not a single relationship but the set of connected propositions that explains why the relationship holds and from which other observations can be derived. Merely adding data or repeating strengthens a generalisation; it does not build a theory.

quiz.takeaway: A hypothesis is a single testable relationship; a theory is the set of connected propositions that explains that relationship and can generate other observations.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Craig’s seven traditions?
quiz.explain: Craig’s seven traditions are rhetorical, semiotic, phenomenological, cybernetic, sociopsychological, sociocultural and critical. “Functionalism” is the subject of another lesson (and is not on Craig’s list). In exams the sociopsychological and sociocultural traditions are often confused.

quiz.prompt: True or false: according to McQuail, media-centric theory mostly sees the media as a reflection of political and economic forces.
quiz.explain: False. That description belongs to society-centric theory. Media-centric theory grants the media more autonomy and influence; it sees them as a primary mover of social change, driven especially by developments in communication technology.

quiz.prompt: In Potter, Cooper and Dupagne’s (1993) journal count, roughly what share of the articles belonged to the critical paradigm?
quiz.explain: The social science paradigm was above 60%, the interpretive about 34%, the critical less than 6%. The first two options are the shares of the other paradigms; “50%” belongs to no paradigm in the data.

quiz.scenario: Imagine: the editor of a local newspaper has for years applied an unwritten rule: “Monday morning, the municipality story doesn’t get read; a sports headline sells.” An academic wants to test this rule in the newspaper’s archive.

parts.prompt: Which of McQuail’s kinds of theory does the editor’s unwritten rule fall under?
parts.explain: The practical knowledge media practitioners accumulate in practice and that guides behaviour is operational theory. Normative theory looks at “how it ought to be,” cultural theory at evaluating or questioning cultural products.

parts.prompt: If the academic will use the results to improve the newspaper’s sales policy, which of Lazarsfeld’s categories is the study closest to?
parts.explain: Research that serves the practical aims of a particular institution is close to Lazarsfeld’s administrative (applied) category. Critical research questions the media’s general role in society and their structure of control; “cultural theory” is not part of Lazarsfeld’s distinction.

parts.prompt: If the academic’s question were “Which interests and power relations does this rule serve?”, which direction would the study move in?
parts.explain: Questioning interests and power relations is the mark of the critical orientation. The administrative orientation serves the institution’s aims; an “operational direction” is not an academic orientation but the name for practitioners’ practical knowledge.

quiz.takeaway: The same phenomenon can be an operational rule, an administrative study or a critical inquiry, depending on for whom and with which question it is examined.

quiz.prompt: What is the core of the “auxiliary hypotheses” criticism of Popper?
options: When a prediction fails, it can remain unclear whether the theory or the auxiliary hypotheses are at fault.
Popper held that testing was unnecessary.
quiz.explain: According to the criticism, auxiliary assumptions stand between theory and observation; when a result is unexpected, it is not easy to tell which one was refuted. The other options distort Popper or the criticism: Popper regarded testing as indispensable.

quiz.prompt: A research team studies a family watching a television news bulletin and treats communication as the “(re)production of social order.” Which of Craig’s traditions is it closest to?
quiz.explain: The tradition that sees communication as the (re)production of social order is the sociocultural tradition. The sociopsychological tradition sees communication as expression, interaction and influence; the cybernetic as information processing; the rhetorical as the practical art of discourse. The pair most often confused is sociopsychological and sociocultural.
